---
title: "Determinant and Inverse — Can We Undo a Transformation?"
description: "An original mathematical walkthrough with one running example, concrete numbers and a proof."
---

## Ask a simple question

The machine scales and mixes two inputs. Can we recover the original inputs from its output?

## Build the intuition

A square matrix has an inverse exactly when it preserves enough information to distinguish every input. A nonzero determinant is the two-dimensional test.

## Write the mathematical relationship

$$
\det\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}=ad-bc
$$

**Every symbol explained:** det is the determinant; a,b,c,d are the four matrix entries. For two dimensions, its absolute value is the scale factor for areas; a zero value indicates collapse to a line or point.

**Substitute real numbers:** For A=[[2,1],[1,−1]], det A=2×(−1)−1×1=−3. Since −3≠0, the inverse exists, and the area scale factor is 3.

## Why the relationship is true

The determinant measures oriented area scaling. If it vanishes, two noncollinear input directions have become dependent, so the mapping cannot be one-to-one.

## Where the shortcut stops working

The determinant alone is not an instruction to divide every matrix entry by it. The inverse of [[a,b],[c,d]] is (1/det)[[d,−b],[−c,a]] for det≠0.

## Your turn

What happens to determinant for B=[[1,2],[2,4]]? Explain why B cannot be inverted.

**Source structure:** Ivan Savov, *No Bullshit Guide to Linear Algebra*, second edition, Computational linear algebra, §§3.4–3.5. This is an independently written explanation based on the uploaded **extended preview**, not a transcription of the commercial full book.
